source: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee, Jurgens (2024) When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts
finding: Telling a model 'you are an expert X' does not raise accuracy on factual questions. It gives no gain or a small loss versus no persona.
numbers: 162 roles (6 interpersonal types, 8 expertise domains); 4 model families; 2,410 MMLU questions across 26 subjects. Most personas not significantly different from the no-persona control, in all models.
quote: adding personas in system prompts does not improve model performance across a range of questions compared to the control setting
limits: Multiple-choice factual QA only; open-source models; not agentic tasks.
agent_relevance: Do not add an 'expert' role line to the schema expecting skill transfer. Surface expertise labels are not expertise.

source: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee, Jurgens (2024) When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts (domain alignment)
finding: A persona matched to the question's domain helps only a little. Lawyer beats doctor on law questions, but the effect is tiny.
numbers: Mixed-effects coefficient for in-domain persona = 0.004 (p<0.01) in accuracy.
limits: Statistically real but practically negligible.
agent_relevance: Domain-specific expert framing gives at most a marginal gain; narrow, not general.

source: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee, Jurgens (2024) When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts (persona search)
finding: Picking the best persona per question after the fact (oracle) beats the control, but automatic selection of that persona does not beat random choice.
numbers: Selection methods tried: random, most-similar role, RoBERTa domain classifier (78.1% domain accuracy), best role on training set, best in-domain role. Predicted-role methods performed about like a random role.
limits: Oracle upper bound uses the answers; not deployable.
agent_relevance: Persona effect looks random per item. Use varied framings with a verifier, not a fixed expert persona.

source: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee, Jurgens (2024) When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts (prompt form)
finding: Audience-style prompts ('you are talking to a lawyer') did slightly better than speaker-style ('you are a lawyer').
numbers: Mixed-effects model; significant but small effect size (Figure 3). Larger Llama3-70B had more personas with negative effects; Qwen2.5-7B and 72B were insensitive to all 162.
limits: Small effects.
agent_relevance: If any role framing is used, address the audience, not the speaker; expect near-zero gain.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does Math Reasoning Improve General LLM Capabilities? Understanding Transferability of LLM Reasoning
finding: Most reasoning-tuned models that excel at math do not carry the gain to other reasoning or to non-reasoning tasks. A direct machine analogue of narrow skill transfer.
numbers: Over 20 open-weight reasoning models evaluated on math, scientific QA, agent planning, coding, instruction following. Introduced a Transferability Index (TI); many models had negative TI on non-reasoning tasks.
quote: most models that succeed in math fail to transfer their gains to other domains
limits: Open-weight models only; recipes differ in several ways, so the survey is correlational.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a strength on one task family (math) applies elsewhere. Test the scaffold per task family.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does Math Reasoning Improve General LLM Capabilities? Understanding Transferability of LLM Reasoning (controlled study)
finding: With the same math-only data on Qwen3-14B-Base, RL tuning transferred but supervised fine-tuning on teacher traces often lost general ability.
numbers: RL model (UniReason-Qwen3-14B): 55.7% AIME24, 87.8% MATH500, 33.8% OlympiadBench; +17.1 points on LiveCodeBench2 over the SFT model; SFT models often had negative non-reasoning TI.
limits: One base model and one math dataset.
agent_relevance: Imitating expert traces narrows; learning from verifiable outcomes kept range. Fits our no-training stance: scaffold, do not fine-tune on narrow expert traces.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does Math Reasoning Improve General LLM Capabilities? Understanding Transferability of LLM Reasoning (mechanism)
finding: Why transfer fails: supervised fine-tuning moves the latent space and token ranks a lot; RL moves them little.
numbers: UniReason-Qwen3-14B (RL) averages only 0.98 positions of token-rank shift; SFT shifts were substantially larger.
limits: One model family for the rank statistic.
agent_relevance: Narrow practice can erode other skills (negative transfer) in machines, a risk if we ever fine-tune.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual Tasks
finding: Across 11 tasks, models did well on the default task but dropped substantially and consistently on a counterfactual twin (same reasoning, unfamiliar rules). Skill is tied to seen conditions.
numbers: 11 tasks (base-9 arithmetic, code, logic, spatial, chess, SET, etc.). GPT-4 chess opening legality, 100 items each: 100% default vs 21% with swapped knight/bishop start, no CoT; with zero-shot CoT 100% vs 61%.
quote: performance substantially and consistently degrades compared to the default conditions
limits: Chess row read from a flattened table; 0-shot CoT narrows but does not close the gap.
agent_relevance: Models resemble human experts who are brittle when the problem shifts. Include re-skinned variants in checks.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual Tasks (control task CCC)
finding: A check of whether the model knows the new rule (CCC) shows models often know it yet still fail the task. The failure is in using knowledge, not in knowing it.
numbers: Chess CCC GPT-4: 89% default vs 74% counterfactual without CoT; 100% vs 96% with CoT. GPT-3.5 chess task: 73% default vs 4% counterfactual without CoT.
limits: Cell-to-model mapping read from flattened text; treat non-GPT-4 cells as approximate.
agent_relevance: The gap between declarative knowledge and use mirrors expert knowledge that does not transfer. A restate-the-rules step helps but does not fix it.

source: Aryabumi et al. (2024) To Code, or Not To Code? Exploring Impact of Code in Pre-training
finding: Counter-case: training on one domain (code) does lift other abilities in models, so transfer is not always absent for machines.
numbers: Models 470M to 2.8B. Versus text-only pretraining, code adds up to 8.2% relative NL reasoning, 4.2% world knowledge, 6.6% generation win rate, 12x code performance. Code-first init beat text-only on NL reasoning by 8.8% (code-text) and 8.2% (balanced-text).
limits: Small models; pretraining, not scaffolding; a 50%-code mix gives up some NL ability.
agent_relevance: Structured formal practice may help broadly, but only when built into training. Prompt-time scaffolds cannot assume it.

source: Berglund et al. (2024) The Reversal Curse
finding: Knowledge learned in one direction ('A is B') is not available in reverse ('B is A') unless it is in context. A clean case of direction-bound learning.
numbers: GPT-4 answers 'Tom Cruise's mother' correctly 79% of the time but the reverse only 33%. Finetuned GPT-3 and Llama-1 on fictitious facts: reverse likelihood no higher than for a random name; not fixed by data augmentation.
quote: if 'A is B' appears in-context, models can deduce the reverse relationship
limits: Fine-tuned facts; in-context reversal works.
agent_relevance: Put needed facts in the working context in the form needed. Do not rely on stored knowledge being retrievable from another angle.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess
finding: A 270M-parameter transformer trained on 10M Lichess games with Stockfish 16 labels, no search, reaches grandmaster-level blitz. Strong skill from one narrow domain with no explicit search.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 against humans; ChessBench has 15 billion annotated data points; 9M, 136M, 270M models compared; puzzles rated 399 to 2867.
limits: Narrow domain; imitation of an engine; perfect distillation not reached; no out-of-domain test.
agent_relevance: Domain skill can be amortised into weights, yet nothing here says it transfers. Supports routing hard domain parts to tools.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models
finding: A GPT trained only on chess text forms board-state and player-skill representations. Adding a skill vector makes it play better.
numbers: 25M (8-layer) and 50M (16-layer) models; skill vector raised win rate vs Stockfish level 0 by up to 2.6 times on random-start boards; board-state edit raised legal-move rate from 41% to 92%; skill probe called 99.4% of 4,000 random-start games low skill.
limits: Small models, one game.
agent_relevance: Skill level is a latent the model infers from context, so context that signals high skill can shift behaviour. This is the mechanism behind persona prompts, but it acts only inside the trained domain.

source: Li et al. (2023) Emergent World Representations: Othello-GPT
finding: A sequence model trained on Othello move text builds an internal board model that can be edited to change its moves. Domain-bound but real.
numbers: Championship set of 7,605 plus 132,921 games and a far larger synthetic set; interventions on the board representation change predicted moves.
limits: Synthetic task; Karvonen notes the probes worked poorly on human-game data in the original.
agent_relevance: Expert-like structure forms from task-specific data; no evidence it carries to other games.

source: Xu et al. (2025) ExpertPrompting: Instructing Large Language Models to be Distinguished Experts
finding: Having a model write a detailed expert identity per question, then answer in that role, got better judged answers than plain answers.
numbers: GPT-4 reviewer preferred expert answers 48.5% vs 23% for vanilla (rest ties); ExpertLLaMA reached 96% of ChatGPT on Vicuna80.
quote: achieves 96% of the original ChatGPT's capability
limits: Judged by GPT-4, not ground truth; open-ended instructions; conflicts with Zheng on MMLU.
agent_relevance: Detailed question-specific expert description may help open-ended quality; a one-line label does not help accuracy. Use only in generation steps.

source: Schut et al. (2023/2025) Bridging the Human-AI Knowledge Gap: Concept Discovery and Transfer in AlphaZero
finding: Concepts pulled from AlphaZero's network and shown as puzzles let four top grandmasters improve. Expertise in a narrow field can be taught from a machine.
numbers: 4 grandmasters (one rated 2600-2700, three 2700-2800). Percent correct, phase 1 to phase 3: GM1 0 to 42, GM2 33 to 58, GM3 25 to 42, GM4 38 to 44; 36 puzzles each, 48 for GM4. Improvement did not follow Elo. 97.6% of concepts removed by teachability filter, a further 27.1% by novelty.
limits: Four people; no control group; same-concept puzzles only; no test of transfer to other concepts.
agent_relevance: Concept prototypes (short worked examples) are a pattern for our worked-example memory.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) EyeMulator: Improving Code Language Models by Mimicking Human Visual Attention
finding: Eye-tracking of programmers used as token weights in fine-tuning gave positive gains in every cell tested. A direct use of expert gaze to train a model.
numbers: Gaze from 27 programmers (EyeTrans, 120Hz); 6 backbones, 2 data regimes, 3 CodeXGLUE tasks: all 36 matched-metric deltas positive; examples +8.0%, +9.7%, +6.8% on one backbone; some cells only +1.4%.
limits: Code tasks, Java; summarization gains smaller.
agent_relevance: For a prompt scaffold the analogue is a 'what to look at first' checklist from expert fixation patterns.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) EyeLayer: Integrating Human Attention Patterns into LLM-Based Code Summarization
finding: A small module built from human gaze patterns improved code summarization across LLaMA-3.2, Qwen3 and CodeBERT.
numbers: Gains up to 13.17% BLEU-4 over fine-tuning baselines.
limits: Summarization only; gains reported as maxima.
agent_relevance: Gaze priors move across models, but within one task type only.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Enhancing Code LLM Training with Programmer Attention
finding: Augmented eye-tracking paths plus a reward in CodeT5 fine-tuning raised summarization scores.
numbers: +7.16 CodeBLEU on CodeXGLUE summarization.
quote: may not fully generalize to completion or translation
limits: Four-page paper; 10% samples of datasets; authors say patterns may not generalize to completion or translation.
agent_relevance: Authors themselves flag narrow transfer even of expert attention.

source: Synthesis of Zheng 2024, Wu 2024, Huan 2025
finding: Across persona, counterfactual, and cross-domain tests, machine skill matches the human expertise finding: strong on trained conditions, narrow beyond them.
numbers: Persona: near-zero gain (Zheng); GPT-4 chess legality 100% to 21% when a rule shifts (Wu); math-tuned models often negative transfer to non-reasoning tasks (Huan).
limits: Different tasks and models; an integration, not one experiment.
agent_relevance: Design rule for the schema: verify per task family; vary the surface of the problem; keep facts in context.

source: Zheng 2024 vs Xu 2025 (conflict note)
finding: Studies disagree on persona benefit because of task and judge: factual multiple choice shows none; open-ended GPT-4-judged answers show a lift.
numbers: Zheng: 2,410 MMLU items, no benefit. Xu: 48.5% vs 23% preference.
limits: Different metrics; the Xu win could be style preference.
agent_relevance: Use ground-truth checks to decide, not model-judge preference.

source: Wu 2024 vs Karvonen 2024 (chess comparison)
finding: General chat models fail a rules twist in chess, while small chess-only models learn board state well. Domain training gives rule fidelity; neither shows flexibility.
numbers: GPT-4 counterfactual chess 21% (no CoT); chess-only GPT board edits raise legal moves 41% to 92%. Different tasks.
limits: Not a direct comparison; different metrics.
agent_relevance: Where rules are fixed, call a tool or rules engine rather than reason from memory.

source: Ruoss 2024 and Schut 2023 (transfer gap)
finding: Machine chess skill (Elo 2895) and machine-taught grandmasters (improvement +6 to +42 points) are both tested only inside chess; neither paper tests transfer out of chess.
numbers: Elo 2895 vs humans; 4 grandmasters, phase 1 to 3 gains of 6 to 42 percentage points.
limits: Absence of a test is not evidence of absence of transfer.
agent_relevance: Open question for our agent; assume narrow until measured.

source: Zheng 2024 (scale note)
finding: Bigger models did not escape persona insensitivity; the largest Llama3-70B had more personas hurt it.
numbers: Llama3-70B: more personas with negative effects; Qwen2.5-72B: insensitive to all 162 personas.
limits: Two or three models, one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Scale alone does not fix persona effects, so do not count on stronger base models to make role labels work.

source: Wu 2024 (CoT boost)
finding: Zero-shot chain-of-thought improves counterfactual performance a lot in some tasks but never fully removes the gap.
numbers: GPT-4 chess counterfactual 21% to 61% with CoT, still below 100% default.
limits: One task row.
agent_relevance: A reasoning scaffold narrows brittleness; keep it, and still test on shifted variants.
